> I leave a local server running my backend projects 24/7, and I want a physical dashboard to monitor its physical environment. I'll use a Raspberry Pi 4, a DHT22 sensor, and some LEDs inside a custom case. The Pi will run a web server so I can check the stats, and the LEDs will alert me if the area around the hardware gets too warm.

## Design

### 2026-10-01 — Spent this session researching the components, planning the stack, and getting the 3D design done.

**6.5h**

Spent this session researching the components, planning the stack, and getting the 3D design done.

After that, I modeled the custom enclosure in Onshape. Knowing the Pi 4 runs warm, I designed ventilation slots and isolated the DHT22 mount so the board heat will not mess with ambient readings. Finally, I exported the STLs, organized the repository into clean /images and /stl folders, and synced everything up.

### 2026-10-01 — Spent this session finalizing the Bill of Materials (BOM) and doing a reality check on local hardware prices. It turns out the Raspberry Pi 4 is way too expensive locally and blows right past the $65

**1.5h**

Spent this session finalizing the Bill of Materials (BOM) and doing a reality check on local hardware prices. It turns out the Raspberry Pi 4 is way too expensive locally and blows right past the $65 Tier 2 funding limit, even before calculating shipping and taxes.

I considered pushing the project to Tier 3, but that requires integrating a motorized component. Forcing a fan or a servo into the build just to get a bigger budget felt like bad engineering and unnecessary complexity for a simple environmental monitor.

Instead of over-engineering the hardware, I decided to pivot the architecture. Since this physical monitor will sit right next to my main 24/7 backend server anyway, I don't need a full Linux board to run a local SQLite database. I'm swapping the Pi 4 out for an ESP32-C6 development board. The ESP32 will act purely as a sensor node, reading the DHT22 and sending HTTP POST requests over Wi-Fi to my existing server, which will handle the Node.js API and data logging. This keeps the project under budget and makes the overall system architecture much cleaner.
